admin-0-done: Well done. You checked the record that every receipt depends on, and you left what was right exactly as it was.
admin-0-intro: Welcome. As the retail administrator, you don't serve customers. But every receipt that leaves this store carries details that you control. The store name. The G S T number. The terminal. Even the width of the paper. Think about that for a moment. Every receipt, and every report, takes these details from one single record. A wrong G S T number prints on every tax invoice. A wrong receipt width can cut off the total. So before the first sale, you check that record. Carefully, and without changing anything that's already right.
admin-0-open: Choose Configure, on Store and terminal.
admin-0-read: Check each field. The store name: Ulundurpet Main Store. The G S T number, the same one printed on every receipt. The terminal: P O S zero one. Receipt width: eighty millimetres. The address on Trichy Main Road. And the default language: English. Tap the button when you've checked them.
admin-0-ready: At the top right, choose View as, Retail administrator. Then open Setup, from the menu on the left.
admin-0-save: Everything is correct, so choose Save, without changing anything.
admin-0-width: The receipt printer for P O S zero one uses eighty millimetre paper. Which receipt width must this record use?
admin-1-done: Perfect. Divya has exactly the access her job needs. Her invitation is on record, and her manager will confirm when she starts.
admin-1-intro: Some good news. Divya is joining Ulundurpet Main Store as a cashier on Monday. Your job is to give her access. And here's the most important rule in your whole role. Access matches the job. Divya needs to sell at the counter. Nothing more. A cashier with administrator rights, or with access to every store, can change prices, users, or stock she was never meant to touch. Giving extra access because it's convenient is exactly how mistakes, and fraud, become possible.
admin-1-invite: In Add named user, type Divya. Set the role to Cashier, and the store scope to Ulundurpet Main Store. Then choose Invite user.
admin-1-open: Choose Configure, on Users and roles.
admin-1-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Setup.
admin-1-scope: Divya asks for access to all stores, just in case. What do you do?
admin-2-done: Good. The settings match what cashiers are taught, and you know who to tell before anything changes.
admin-2-drawer: Now choose Configure, on Cash drawer. Check that the opening float is two thousand five hundred, and that the drawer opens after every cash payment. Then choose Save.
admin-2-intro: In the cashier course, Kavya learns two simple facts. P O S zero one opens with two thousand five hundred rupees in the drawer. And it accepts cash, U P I, card and split payments. But where do those facts come from? They come from settings that you own. And that's why this lesson matters. If the drawer setting says one thing, and the cashiers are taught another, every single shift starts with a cash difference that nobody can explain.
admin-2-pay: Choose Configure, on Payments. Check that cash, U P I, card, and split tender are all ticked, and that the timeout is ninety seconds. Everything is right, so choose Cancel, to leave it unchanged.
admin-2-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Setup.
admin-2-tell: Imagine you change the opening float to three thousand rupees. Who must know before the next shift?
admin-3-cert: The matrix says no hardware is production-certified, and the scanner shows physical certification pending. So what do you tell the store?
admin-3-done: That's an honest answer. The scanner works in a test, and certification is still pending. Now the store manager can make the right decision.
admin-3-intro: The store manager calls you. Is the barcode scanner on P O S zero one ready for live sales? It's a simple question. But be careful with the answer. A device that passes a test is not the same as a device that's certified for live trading. Certification checks the real device, its driver, its firmware, and the store's network. If you call a demo device ready, the first real failure will happen with a customer standing at the counter. So let's test it, and then check what it's actually certified for.
admin-3-matrix: The test passed. Now close it, and choose Open assurance matrix.
admin-3-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Setup.
admin-3-scan: Choose Configure, on Barcode scanner. Then scan, or type, the milk barcode: eight, nine, zero, one, zero, zero, two. And press Enter.
admin-4-done: Well done. You checked the store record, gave the right access, kept the cash and payment settings honest, told the truth about device certification, and protected the warnings everyone relies on. Next, we'll add a product.
admin-4-intro: Every morning, the owner and the store manager open the Signals screen. It tells them what needs attention today. But here's something they may not realise. The rules that decide what appears there belong to you. Set a rule too loose, and real problems stay hidden. Set it too tight, and managers are flooded with warnings until they stop reading them. Today, for example, Ponni rice is on the screen because demand is thirty-two percent above plan, and the rule alerts above twenty-five percent. Switch that rule off, and that warning quietly disappears, for everyone.
admin-4-read: Read the four rules. Stock-out risk, when cover falls below two days. Expiry risk, seven days before expiry. Demand surge, when demand is twenty-five percent above plan. And inventory variance, when the shelf and the system disagree. Tap the button when you've read them.
admin-4-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Signals.
admin-4-save: Keep all four rules switched on, and choose Save.
admin-4-which: Sunflower oil shows a stock-out risk in one point four days. Which rule raised it?
admin-5-check: Check the catalogue list. Barcodes ending one to eight are already in use. The curd's barcode, ending ninety-nine, is not. Tap the button when you've checked.
admin-5-create: Choose Add product. Enter the barcode, eight nine zero one zero nine nine. The name, Aavin Curd 400g. The price, thirty-five. Opening stock, zero. And the category, Dairy. Then choose Create product.
admin-5-done: Well done. One new product, one new barcode, and no stock claimed until the goods actually arrive.
admin-5-dup: Suppose the invoice had shown the milk's barcode, eight nine zero one zero zero two, for the curd. What would you do?
admin-5-intro: Remember the cashier who scanned the Aavin curd, and got product not found? That report has reached you. The supplier's invoice lists it: Aavin curd, four hundred grams, barcode eight nine zero one zero nine nine, selling at thirty-five rupees. Your job is to add it. Here's the one rule you must never break. One barcode, one product. If you reuse a barcode that already belongs to something else, every scan sells the wrong product. And this screen won't stop you. So you check first.
admin-5-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Catalogue.
admin-5-zero: Why is the opening stock zero?
admin-6-disable: Find Suresh, cashier, active. And choose Disable. Only Suresh.
admin-6-done: Exactly right. The door is closed, and the change is on record.
admin-6-intro: Suresh, a cashier at Ulundurpet, finished his last shift today. He's left the company. Now, his account still works. And an account belongs to a job, not to a person forever. A leaver's active account is an open door. Anyone who knows the password can sell, refund, or approve, under his name. So the account closes when the job ends. Today.
admin-6-open: Choose Configure, on Users and roles.
admin-6-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Setup.
admin-6-when: When should a leaver's access be removed?
admin-7-done: And that completes the administrator's course. You found the failed event, and you confirmed it was fixed exactly once. That's how stock stays true across every store.
admin-7-intro: This afternoon, something went wrong between two systems. A stock message failed, and was moved to a dead-letter queue. That's a holding area, for messages the system couldn't process. Why should you care? Because when a message fails quietly, stock in one store can fall out of step with another. So you find the failed event, and you check one important thing. When it was fixed, was it applied exactly once? Apply it twice, and the same goods are counted twice.
admin-7-once: Why does destination stock updated once matter?
admin-7-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Retail administrator, and open Observability.
admin-7-timeline: Now read the incident timeline. It failed at two minutes past two. It was retried three times, then moved to the dead-letter queue. It was replayed at eight minutes past two, after a correction. And it completed, with the destination stock updated once. Tap the button when you've read it.
admin-7-trace: Finally, choose Trace, on the failed event, to open its trace.
admin-7-which: Read the table. Which event failed, and was moved to the dead-letter queue?
backoffice-0-big: Why can't you approve the thirty-two thousand rupee refund?
backoffice-0-done: Well done. You approved what was yours to approve, and left the large refund to the owner. Next, Finance checks what actually happened.
backoffice-0-intro: You are Kumar, the payment approver. Four customer refunds are waiting, from two hundred and thirty-eight rupees, up to thirty-two thousand. Your limit is ten thousand rupees per refund. A refund sends the business's money out. So limits make sure larger amounts get a more senior decision, and anything very large is checked by a second person. And one rule never bends: you never approve a refund you asked for yourself.
backoffice-0-mid: On RF five zero three, eight thousand four hundred rupees for a cancelled bulk order, choose Approve. It's within your limit.
backoffice-0-next: So who checks that the approved money really left the business?
backoffice-0-read: Read the queue. Four refunds, and the line at the top saying you approve up to ten thousand rupees. The thirty-two thousand rupee refund shows Above your limit, instead of buttons. Tap the button when you've read it.
backoffice-0-role: Choose View as: Payment approver at the top right. Then open Refunds and payments in the left menu.
backoffice-0-small: On RF five zero one, two hundred and thirty-eight rupees for a gateway that charged twice, choose Approve.
backoffice-1-approve: There are no Approve buttons for you on this screen. Why not?
backoffice-1-diff: Suppose the report had shown two hundred and eighty-three rupees instead of two hundred and thirty-eight. What should you do?
backoffice-1-done: Well done. The refund is closed in the books, matched to a real payment. Next, we'll see the whole journey from the customer's side.
backoffice-1-intro: You are Anitha, in Finance. Kumar approved a refund of two hundred and thirty-eight rupees. The payment gateway's settlement report shows it under a reference number. Reconciling proves that the money approved is the money that actually moved. It catches refunds paid twice, paid to the wrong customer, or never paid at all.
backoffice-1-recon: On RF five zero one, choose Reconcile. Type the reference exactly as the report shows it, U T R, dash, four four seven one zero nine two three one eight four six. Then choose Reconcile.
backoffice-1-role: Choose View as: Finance and accounts. Then open Refunds and payments.
backoffice-2-add: Choose Immediate delivery. Then choose Add on Aavin milk, twice.
backoffice-2-approve: Now switch View as to Payment approver. Open Refunds and payments, and approve Priya's refund, at the top of the list.
backoffice-2-chat: Make sure WhatsApp is selected. Keep the number shown, and choose Start chat.
backoffice-2-deliver: In My orders, choose Simulate next step, until the order shows Delivered.
backoffice-2-done: Well done. Priya's leaking packet became a refund, approved by Kumar, within his limit. Every step, from her phone to the books, was checked. In the last lesson, Priya sets up a weekly plan.
backoffice-2-express: Why would Express delivery, with cash on delivery, have been refused?
backoffice-2-intro: Priya orders milk on WhatsApp. After delivery, one packet is leaking, and she asks for a refund. In this lesson you follow her order, from her phone, all the way to the store's refund queue. Seeing the customer's side shows why every rule matters. Stock reservations, delivery rules and refund limits are each a promise to a real person.
backoffice-2-order: Beside the chat, in Immediate delivery, keep the delivery as Express, and set the payment to U P I. Then choose Place order.
backoffice-2-return: Choose Return an item. Keep Aavin milk, quantity one, and the reason Damaged or leaking. Then choose Request return.
backoffice-2-role: Choose View as: Customer, shop view. Then open Customer shop.
backoffice-3-add: Under Suggested for weekly plan, add Aavin milk twice, and red onion, one kilo, once.
backoffice-3-away: Priya is away next Saturday, but wants her plan to carry on after that. What should she do?
backoffice-3-done: And that completes the course. Priya's weekly plan runs by itself, she can skip or pause it in a tap, and each delivery reaches the store as a normal order, with stock reserved. Well done.
backoffice-3-intro: Priya wants two packets of milk and a kilo of onions every Saturday morning, without ordering each week. She uses the mobile app. Plans bring steady, predictable orders. The store can plan its stock and its delivery runs, and the customer saves time. But only if skipping, pausing and changing the plan are easy. Otherwise customers cancel, or refuse deliveries at the door.
backoffice-3-role: Choose View as: Customer, shop view. Then open Customer shop.
backoffice-3-run: Now choose Delivery day, practice. The plan becomes an order for the store, and appears in My orders.
backoffice-3-signin: Choose Sign in to start. Sign in with the email priya at example dot com, and the password priya dash pass dash one.
backoffice-3-skip: In My plans, choose Skip next delivery. The next delivery moves on by a week.
backoffice-3-start: Set the delivery day to Every Saturday, the time slot to Morning, seven to nine, and the payment to U P I Autopay. Then choose Start weekly plan.
backoffice-3-store: Where does the store see this delivery?
backoffice-3-tab: Choose the Mobile app tab. In the app, choose Weekly plan.
cashier-0-done: Well done. Your counter is ready, and you know exactly how much cash you started with. In the next lesson, your first customer arrives.
cashier-0-float: One more. How much cash should be in your drawer before your first sale?
cashier-0-intro: Good morning. Before we touch the screen, let me tell you a short story. It is eight o'clock at AIFirstMart, Ulundurpet Main Store. You are Kavya, and you look after the billing counter, terminal P O S zero one. In a few minutes the doors open, and your first customer will want a quick and correct bill. So before anyone arrives, you get your counter ready. Why does this matter? Because every bill you make carries your name, your terminal, and the time. And at the end of the day, your cash is checked against the two thousand five hundred rupees you started with. If that starting count is wrong, an honest shift can look short, or over. Nobody else receives your work yet. A ready terminal and a counted drawer are simply what you need for your very first sale. Let's begin.
cashier-0-look: Now look at the bar across the top. In this practice system, it says Online, Demo scanner, and Printer not certified. In the real store, the scanner and the printer must both be ready before your first sale. When you have looked, tap the button in the panel.
cashier-0-printer: Here's a question for you. In the real store, the printer says not certified. What would you do?
cashier-0-ready: First, make sure the system knows who you are. At the top right, choose View as, Cashier. Then, in the menu on the left, open Sell.
cashier-1-done: Perfect. Two lines, exact quantities, and the right subtotal. Next, you'll apply a discount, and see what happens when a discount goes too far.
cashier-1-empty: We always start with an empty basket. If anything is already in it, choose New sale.
cashier-1-intro: It is a quarter past ten. A customer walks up to your counter and puts down two packets of Aavin milk, five hundred millilitres each, and a one kilogram pack of red onions. This little basket matters more than it looks. It becomes the customer's bill. It reduces the shop's stock. And it is written into the audit record. So every line has to be exact. Imagine you tap the onion tile twice by mistake. The customer would pay forty-two rupees more. And the stock record would show a second kilo of onions leaving the shelf, when it never did. Small, yes. But repeated all day, across every counter, it adds up. So let's build this basket carefully.
cashier-1-milk: Now scan the milk. Type the barcode, eight, nine, zero, one, zero, zero, two, into the scan box, and press Enter. Then do it once more, for the second packet. You can also tap the Aavin Milk tile twice.
cashier-1-onion: Now the onions. This is a one kilogram pack, and the customer has just one. Type its barcode, eight, nine, zero, one, zero, zero, seven, into the scan box, and press Enter. Or, if you can see the Red Onion one kg tile, tap it once. It costs forty-two rupees.
cashier-1-ready: Check that you are viewing as Cashier, and that the Sell screen is open.
cashier-1-sub: Let's check your work. Milk: two packets at twenty-six rupees, that's fifty-two rupees. Onions: one pack, forty-two rupees. Subtotal: ninety-four rupees. Compare each line on the screen. When it all matches, tap, I have checked the basket.
cashier-2-apply: Now the real offer. Choose Add again. Type five, pick the reason Loyalty offer, and apply it. Five rupees is well within your limit, so it goes straight onto the bill.
cashier-2-done: Nicely done. You saw the limit working, and you applied the right discount. Now, let's take the payment, safely.
cashier-2-intro: Your basket comes to ninety-four rupees. The customer smiles and shows you a loyalty offer worth five rupees. Here's something every good cashier learns early. The discount box on this screen takes rupees, not percent. Type five, and the customer gets five rupees off. Not five percent. On your own, you can give up to ten percent of the bill. Anything above that goes to a supervisor, and you can never approve your own request. Why so strict? Because every small discount at the counter adds up to the discount figure the owner reads every single morning. Let's try it. And first, let's see what happens when we go over the limit.
cashier-2-over: First, let's test the limit. Next to Discount, choose Add. Type twelve, and choose Apply, or request approval. Twelve rupees is more than ten percent of this bill. So watch what the system does.
cashier-2-own: The twelve rupee request is now waiting for approval. So, who can approve it?
cashier-2-ready: Make sure you are on the Sell screen as Cashier, with the basket from the last lesson still there.
cashier-2-total: Look at the basket now. What is the total the customer has to pay?
cashier-3-done: Excellent. You completed the sale only after the terminal confirmed it. That one habit protects the shop from payments that never arrive.
cashier-3-intro: The total is ninety-three rupees, forty-five paise, and the customer wants to pay by U P I. This is the moment where a lot of mistakes happen. A customer holds up their phone and says, it's done, it's gone through. And it's tempting to believe them. But here is the rule. Only the payment terminal's confirmation proves the shop has been paid. When you press Complete sale, the shop records that the money has arrived. If the payment actually failed, the customer walks out with goods the shop was never paid for. And nobody finds out until settlement, days later. So in this lesson, you wait for the terminal. Every time.
cashier-3-pay: Now wait for the terminal. In this practice, its confirmation appears in the dark box in the panel. Type that reference number into the field, Amount received, or authorization reference, replacing the amount. Then choose Complete sale.
cashier-3-ready: Check that you are on the Sell screen as Cashier, with the five rupee discount still applied.
cashier-3-upi: Choose U P I. The customer now scans the Q R code on the payment terminal.
cashier-4-done: And that's a complete, careful sale, from an empty basket to a correct receipt. Well done, Kavya.
cashier-4-intro: The payment has gone through. Now comes the last part of the sale, and it's easy to rush. Only a completed sale really counts. It's the record that the customer paid, that stock left the shop, and who made the sale. And your sale now travels on. Inventory uses it to reduce the stock. Finance uses it to settle the U P I payment. Even your five rupee discount goes into the audit trail, and becomes part of the figure the owner reviews. So before you turn to the next customer, you check the receipt, and you close this sale properly.
cashier-4-missing: Here's a little puzzle. The item lines add up to ninety-four rupees. But the total says ninety-three rupees forty-five. What's missing from this practice receipt?
cashier-4-next: Hand over the receipt, and choose Next sale. The basket empties, and the sale number goes up by one. Remember, closing here means finishing this one bill. Closing your shift is a separate step, with your supervisor.
cashier-4-paid: This lesson continues from the sale you completed in the last lesson.
cashier-4-read: Look at the receipt. It should show the store name, the G S T number, the receipt number, your name and the time, both items, a total of ninety-three rupees forty-five, and Paid by U P I. When you have checked it, tap the button in the panel.
cashier-5-change: The customer gave you fifty rupees, for a total of twenty-nine rupees forty. How much change is due?
cashier-5-done: Well done. You recorded the cash you actually received, and you worked out the change yourself. That's a cash sale that will balance at closing.
cashier-5-due: Look at the basket. What is the total due?
cashier-5-empty: We start with an empty basket. If anything is already in it, choose New sale.
cashier-5-intro: Not every customer pays by phone. Here's one paying the old way. A customer buys a packet of Tata salt, one kilogram, and hands you a fifty rupee note. Now, cash is special. It's the one payment the system cannot check for you. The amount you type, and the change you hand back, are the only record of what really happened at your counter. So if you type the total instead of the note you received, or you count the change wrong, nobody will find out until closing time, when the drawer doesn't match, and nobody can say why.
cashier-5-next: Hand over the change and the receipt, then choose Next sale.
cashier-5-pay: Choose Pay, and choose Cash. Now type fifty, the note the customer handed you, into Amount received. Not the total. Fifty. Then choose Complete sale.
cashier-5-ready: Make sure you are on the Sell screen as Cashier.
cashier-5-salt: Scan the salt. Type eight, nine, zero, one, zero, zero, four, and press Enter. Just once.
cashier-6-add: Scan the biscuits. Type eight, nine, zero, one, zero, zero, six, and press Enter, once.
cashier-6-done: Perfect. Her basket came back exactly as she left it, and the queue never had to wait.
cashier-6-empty: We start with an empty basket. If anything is already in it, choose New sale.
cashier-6-hold: Now choose Hold. Watch the basket empty, and Held sales change to one.
cashier-6-intro: Here's a moment every cashier knows. A customer has a packet of Marie Gold biscuits on your counter, and then she pats her pockets. Her wallet is in the car. And there's someone waiting right behind her. You could clear the basket and start again later, from memory. But that's exactly how items get missed, or charged twice. Instead, you hold the sale. It keeps her basket safe, and lets you serve the next customer straight away.
cashier-6-ready: Make sure you are on the Sell screen as Cashier.
cashier-6-resume: She's back, with her wallet. Choose Held sales, then Resume, on the held sale of thirty-six rupees seventy-five.
cashier-6-where: The basket is empty now. So where is the first customer's packet of biscuits?
cashier-7-done: That's the right call. The catalogue team now has a review task, and no wrong price went on anybody's bill.
cashier-7-empty: We start with an empty basket. If anything is already in it, choose New sale.
cashier-7-intro: A customer hands you a pot of Aavin curd, four hundred grams. You scan it, and the screen says: product not found. It's tempting, isn't it? Scan a similar product with a known price, and keep the queue moving. But please don't. Every product must exist in the catalogue, with its own price and its own tax. Selling it under another product's barcode makes the bill wrong, the tax wrong, and the stock wrong, for two products at once. The right move is to report it.
cashier-7-ready: Make sure you are on the Sell screen as Cashier.
cashier-7-report: The system says it's not in the catalogue. In Product name, type Aavin Curd 400g, exactly as it's printed on the pot. Then choose Submit for review.
cashier-7-scan: Type the curd's barcode, eight, nine, zero, one, zero, nine, nine, into the scan box, and press Enter.
cashier-7-similar: One quick question. Can you sell the curd by scanning a similar product with a known price?
cashier-8-done: Well done. The right item, the right receipt, and the money going back the way it came.
cashier-8-find: Choose Return. Check the receipt number: P O S zero one, one zero four two. Set the reason to Damaged product. Then choose Find receipt.
cashier-8-intro: A customer comes back to your counter with a bag of Aashirvaad atta, five kilograms. The bag is torn. She bought it on receipt P O S zero one, one zero four two. That same receipt also shows two packets of Tata salt. She's keeping those. A return reverses part of a sale. Money goes back to the customer, and the item comes back into the shop's records. So it must match the original receipt exactly. Refunding without the receipt, refunding things the customer is keeping, or paying cash for a card sale, are the most common ways money leaves a shop by mistake.
cashier-8-items: Tick only the atta, two hundred and ninety-four rupees. Leave the salt unticked, because she's keeping it. Keep the refund method as Original payment method. Then choose Complete return.
cashier-8-method: The atta was paid for by card. So why do we refund to the original payment method?
cashier-8-ready: Make sure you are on the Sell screen as Cashier.
fb-wrong: Not quite. Read the explanation, and try again.
manager-0-cover: Shift coverage shows one gap at four o'clock. When do you act?
manager-0-done: Good. You know the day's numbers, you've spotted the gap early, and you know who is waiting for you. That's a store manager who's ahead of the day.
manager-0-intro: Good morning, Raj. It's eight o'clock, and you're the store manager at Ulundurpet Main Store. In an hour, the doors open. Before that happens, you need to know one thing: can today run safely? Think of it like this. Everything your cashier, your pickers and your riders do today depends on the plan you check right now. A gap you spot at eight in the morning is one phone call. The same gap, found at four in the afternoon, is a queue of unhappy customers. So let's look at the day, before the day looks at us.
manager-0-read: Read the four figures. Sales today: one point eight four lakh rupees, ninety-four percent of target. Open orders: twenty-three, with five due in the next hour. Pending approvals: four, and the oldest has been waiting eighteen minutes. And shift coverage: eleven of twelve, with one gap at four o'clock. Tap the button when you've read them.
manager-0-ready: At the top right, choose View as, Store manager. Then open Command center, from the menu on the left.
manager-0-wait: Four approvals are waiting, and the oldest has waited eighteen minutes. Why does that matter?
manager-1-assign: On Priya's order, ending eighty-eight twenty-one, choose Assign order. Set the picker to Meena, and the packer to Meena. For the picker device, choose Mobile P M zero two. P M zero three is already in Arun's hands. Then choose Assign and send.
manager-1-cap: Choose Team capacity, and read who is busy right now. Then choose Done.
manager-1-done: Well done. The order is with someone who is free, on a device that's free, and it's already on Meena's phone. Priya's promise is safe.
manager-1-free: Arun is picking one order. Kavya is packing one. And Meena is available. So, who takes Priya's order?
manager-1-intro: It's ten to one. Priya has placed a WhatsApp order: eight items, worth one thousand two hundred and eighty-six rupees, and she chose express delivery for one thirty-five. But look at the order queue. Nobody has been assigned to pick it. Here's the thing about an unassigned order. Nobody is picking it. Every minute it waits comes straight out of Priya's promise time. And there's a trap here too. Assigning it to someone who is already busy, or to a scanner someone else is using, makes it look handled when it isn't. So first, we check who is actually free.
manager-1-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Orders from the menu on the left.
manager-2-after: Meena counted thirty packets of milk, but the system shows thirty-two. So what happens to the stock record now?
manager-2-count: Choose Start count. Keep the scope as low-stock products, and assign it to Meena. Now replace the numbers with what Meena actually counted: atta eighteen, milk thirty, rice eleven, salt forty-four. Then choose Submit count.
manager-2-done: Exactly right. You recorded what was really on the shelf, and the difference has gone for approval and investigation. Nothing was hidden.
manager-2-intro: Meena has finished the low-stock count, and her sheet reads: atta, eighteen. Milk, thirty. Rice, eleven. Salt, forty-four. But the system says there should be thirty-two packets of milk. Two are missing. Now, why does a small difference like that matter? Because the stock on the screen decides what customers can order online. If the system thinks there are thirty-two packets, and the shelf only has thirty, two customers may be promised milk that simply isn't there. And here's the temptation. The count boxes on this screen already show the system's numbers. It would be easy to leave them, and make the difference disappear. Don't. A hidden difference hides theft, damage, or a receiving mistake.
manager-2-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Stock.
manager-3-decide: The system refused. Good. Now sign as yourself. Choose Raj, store manager, as the approver. Keep the step-up authentication. Set the decision to Reject, because no reason was given. Then choose Sign and commit decision.
manager-3-done: That's an independent, signed decision, with your name and manager I D on record. Kavya can resubmit with a reason, and the limit stays a real limit.
manager-3-intro: A request is waiting. Kavya, your cashier, has asked for a twelve percent discount, worth one hundred and eighty-six rupees. Her limit is ten percent, and no reason has been recorded. Now, an approval only protects the shop when the person deciding is not the person asking. This system enforces that. But only if every approver signs in as themselves. So in this lesson, we'll first watch the control refuse the wrong person. Then you'll make the decision yourself, properly signed.
manager-3-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Approvals.
manager-3-sod: Let's test the control. Choose Independent approval. Set the approver to Kavya, the person who asked. Then choose Sign and commit decision. Watch what the system does.
manager-4-close: Choose Close and reconcile shift. Type the cash you counted: four two zero zero. Set the variance reason to Cash shortage. Write a short note about what you checked. Then choose Close and settle.
manager-4-done: And that's an honest close. The real count, the right reason, and a note, all on record for Finance. That's how a store day really ends.
manager-4-intro: It's nine o'clock at night. The store is closed, and the system expects four thousand two hundred and fifty rupees in cash for P O S zero one. You count the drawer with Kavya, carefully. Four thousand two hundred rupees. Fifty rupees short. Now, here's what separates a good manager from a tired one. A tired manager types the expected amount and goes home. The shift looks balanced. And the shortage disappears. A good manager records the real count, and the reason. Fifty rupees is easy to explain tonight. Found a week from now, it never will be.
manager-4-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Sell.
manager-4-var: You counted four thousand two hundred rupees. The system expects four thousand two hundred and fifty. What is the variance?
manager-5-decide: Now record exactly what Fathima said. The substitute: Heritage milk, plus two rupees. Her decision: approved in WhatsApp. And the price: charge the difference, because she accepted it. Then choose Confirm decision.
manager-5-done: Exactly right. Her consent is on record, the order is repriced, and the picker knows what to pick.
manager-5-intro: Fathima has placed a WhatsApp order, and one item is a problem. Aavin milk isn't available for her order. Your team offered her Heritage milk instead, which costs two rupees more. And Fathima replied on WhatsApp: yes, Heritage is fine. Now, why does her reply matter so much? Because a substitute changes what she receives, and what she pays. Only her recorded answer makes that change fair. It also protects the shop if she complains later. Swapping or repricing without consent turns a helpful idea into a complaint, and a refund.
manager-5-noreply: Imagine Fathima had not replied by the time picking starts. Which decision would you record?
manager-5-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Orders.
manager-6-decide: Set the reason to Customer unavailable. Set the resolution to Schedule reattempt. Keep the bags in return staging. And notify her by WhatsApp and the app. Then choose Apply resolution.
manager-6-done: Good decision. Her order goes out again, her goods are safe, and she's been told what happens next.
manager-6-intro: A delivery has failed. The customer wasn't home, and the rider has brought the bags back to the store. The good news: she's replied that she'll be home this evening. A failed delivery leaves three loose ends at once. The customer still wants her order. The goods are waiting, and some of them may be chilled. And the payment must stay matched. Your decision ties all three together. Leave the bags without a decision, and the customer is neither delivered to, nor refunded.
manager-6-open: Choose Open exception, on Failed delivery.
manager-6-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Logistics.
manager-6-why: Why hold the bags in return staging, instead of putting them back on the shelves?
manager-7-create: She agrees. Set the fulfilment to Planned Delivery, keep the payment as C O D, and choose Validate and create.
manager-7-done: Nicely handled. Lakshmi gets her groceries this afternoon, paying the way she wanted, and the shop's rule stays intact.
manager-7-intro: The phone rings. It's Lakshmi. She wants the Essentials basket, six items worth eight hundred and forty-six rupees. She wants it delivered express. And she wants to pay cash on delivery. Here's the thing. The shop's rule is that express delivery must be paid in advance. If you promise her express with cash before checking, you'll have to call her back and disappoint her. So let's see the rule for ourselves, and then offer her a choice that works.
manager-7-offer: Lakshmi still wants to pay cash. So what can you offer her?
manager-7-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Orders.
manager-7-try: Choose Create order. Keep Lakshmi and the Essentials basket. Set the fulfilment to Express Delivery, and the payment to C O D. Then choose Validate and create, and read what the system says.
manager-8-done: Well done. The stock went up by exactly what arrived, with the batch and expiry on record.
manager-8-intro: The Aavin distributor has arrived with a delivery. The invoice says twenty-four packets of milk. Before anything goes into the system, you count them. Twenty-four. Good. And you note the batch and expiry printed on the packets. Here's why we're so careful. Stock should only go up when goods are physically in the store, and checked. An invoice proves what was billed. It doesn't prove what arrived. Post the invoice number without counting, and any shortage gets paid for, and then turns up later as a mysterious loss.
manager-8-post: Choose Receive stock. Set the supplier to Aavin Distributor. The purchase order is P O, twenty twenty-six, zero nine one eight. The product: Aavin milk, five hundred millilitres. The quantity: twenty-four. And type the batch and expiry from the packets: A V one zero zero one, expiry the fourth of October, twenty twenty-six. Then choose Post receipt.
manager-8-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Stock.
manager-8-short: Imagine you had counted only twenty-two packets. What would you post?
manager-9-adjust: Choose Inventory operations. On Adjustment, choose Aavin milk. Enter minus one. Set the reason to Damage, write-off. Then choose Post adjustment.
manager-9-done: Exactly. A known loss, recorded with its reason. No mystery at the next count.
manager-9-intro: While the milk is being shelved, one packet slips, and bursts. It can't be sold. It's just one packet. But if it stays in the system, the store will promise a customer milk it doesn't have. And at the next count, there'll be a difference nobody can explain. Record it now, while you know exactly what happened.
manager-9-now: Why record the minus one now, instead of letting the next count find it?
manager-9-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Store manager, and open Stock.
owner-0-done: Good. You read sales and margin together, and you spotted the discount leakage. That's exactly where a careful owner looks first.
owner-0-intro: Let's step into the owner's shoes. It's nine in the morning. You own AIFirstMart, and before you speak to any of your managers, you open the Command center. Here's a lesson many owners learn the hard way. Sales going up is not always good news. If you're also giving away more in discounts than you planned, part of that growth may have been bought with discounts. Sales tell you what came in. Contribution tells you what the shop actually kept. So you never read one number on its own. You read them in pairs.
owner-0-leak: Now look at your priority work. Which item tells you that part of the sales growth may have come from discounts?
owner-0-read: Read the four figures in pairs. Net sales: eight point four two lakh rupees, seven point eight percent above plan. Read that together with contribution: one point seven six lakh rupees. Then orders at risk: seven, with three that need action. Read that together with stock health: ninety-two percent. Tap the button when you're done.
owner-0-ready: At the top right, choose View as, Business owner. Then open Command center, from the menu on the left.
owner-0-share: Let's do a little arithmetic. Contribution is one point seven six lakh, on sales of eight point four two lakh. What share of sales did the shop keep?
owner-1-done: Well judged. Routine work stays with its owner, and the unusual signal gets a closer look, with evidence.
owner-1-intro: Your Signals screen shows three warnings this morning. Sunflower oil may run out in one point four days. Twelve packets of Aavin milk are close to expiry. And Ponni rice is selling thirty-two percent above plan. Now, here's the owner's real skill. It is not fixing everything yourself. If you jump on every signal, you end up doing your managers' work, and they stop owning it. But if you ignore them all, a wrong plan can keep causing shortages, month after month. So for each signal, you ask two simple questions. Who already owns it? And does it really need my decision?
owner-1-oil: Sunflower oil may run out in one point four days. Who should raise the reorder?
owner-1-read: Read the three signals and their priority. Notice that the action column is empty for you. That's on purpose. Those actions belong to the inventory and pricing teams. Tap the button when you're ready.
owner-1-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Signals from the menu on the left.
owner-1-rice: Ponni rice is selling thirty-two percent above plan. That's beyond the twenty-five percent alert. What do you do first?
owner-2-deny: In the Operational approvals panel, find the discount of one hundred and eighty-six rupees, requested by Kavya. Nothing follows her name, because no reason was given. Without a business reason, the right decision is Deny, so that Kavya can resubmit it, with a reason. And don't use the Review link on the table row. That older window doesn't record anything.
owner-2-done: Good decision. It's on record, and Kavya knows exactly what to do next. That's how a limit stays a real limit.
owner-2-intro: A request is waiting for you. Kavya, the cashier, has asked for a discount worth one hundred and eighty-six rupees. But look closely. The reason is empty. One discount like this feels small. But remember the warning on your Command center, discount leakage above plan? That figure is simply many small decisions like this one, added together. If you approve requests without a reason, your team learns that the ten percent limit is just a suggestion. So today, you make the decision the policy expects.
owner-2-limit: Let's work out what this request really means. One hundred and eighty-six rupees is twelve percent of a bill of one thousand five hundred and fifty rupees. What is the cashier's ten percent limit on that bill?
owner-2-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Approvals.
owner-3-books: The cash total is right. But what must Finance still record?
owner-3-cod: Find the cash on delivery amount, four thousand two hundred and eighty rupees, next to Riders and collections. That's the cash customers paid the rider. Tap the button when you've found it.
owner-3-done: Well done. You checked the gross amounts, not just the cash. That's how hidden errors get caught.
owner-3-intro: Arun, one of the RapidGo delivery riders, has collected four thousand two hundred and eighty rupees, cash on delivery, from customers. His rider statement shows he's owed six hundred and eighty rupees: five hundred and sixty in delivery fees, and one hundred and twenty as an incentive. So he hands over three thousand six hundred rupees. The cash adds up. But here's the trap. If only the three thousand six hundred is recorded, your sales look six hundred and eighty rupees lower than they really were, and the delivery cost quietly disappears. The business looks worse on sales, and better on costs, than it really is. Two mistakes that cancel each other out. That's why you check the full picture, not just the cash.
owner-3-net: So, how much cash should Arun hand over?
owner-3-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Logistics from the menu on the left.
owner-3-stmt: Now choose Rider statement. It shows five hundred and sixty rupees in fees, plus one hundred and twenty incentive. Six hundred and eighty rupees payable.
owner-4-done: Well done. You read the numbers in pairs, kept routine work with its owners, held the line on policy, checked the evidence, and put your decision on record. That's good governance. Next, we'll look for patterns.
owner-4-find: Type the word Denied into Search audit. Your decision from the approvals lesson will appear: a denied discount of one hundred and eighty-six rupees.
owner-4-intro: You've had a busy morning. You've read the business health, sorted the signals, decided on a discount request, and checked the cash. Now comes the step that's easiest to skip: writing down what you decided. A decision without an owner and a review date is really just an opinion. When the next review comes around, nobody can say whether it worked. And the same problem comes back next month, as if for the first time.
owner-4-parts: Last question. Which four parts make a decision complete?
owner-4-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Audit.
owner-5-act: Kavya's name is on two exceptions in the history, and on a pending discount. So what do you do?
owner-5-done: Well judged. You found the pattern, and you'll raise it with evidence, fairly.
owner-5-hist: Now choose Approval history, and read the four past requests.
owner-5-intro: Your Command center said discount leakage is above plan. Before your weekly meeting with Raj, you look at recent approval requests. And here's what an owner looks for. Not single decisions. Patterns. One exception is just a decision. The same name, or the same kind of request, appearing again and again, is a pattern. And patterns are what an owner manages. But be fair. A pattern is a reason to ask questions, with evidence. It is not a verdict.
owner-5-name: Look at the Owner column in the history. Whose name is on two rows?
owner-5-pending: Read the two pending requests, and who asked. A twelve percent discount, requested by Kavya. And a void sale for seven hundred and forty-two rupees, requested by Arun. Remember those two names, because the history window will cover this table. Tap the button when you're ready.
owner-5-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Approvals.
owner-6-after: Ulundurpet had twenty-four, and sent twelve. Kallakurichi had seven. What do they hold after the oil arrives?
owner-6-done: Exactly right. Twelve bottles, counted once, in one place at a time.
owner-6-intro: Twelve bottles of sunflower oil are moving from Ulundurpet to Kallakurichi. It sounds simple. But here's where stock goes wrong. Each store's figure must change exactly once. The sending store, when the goods leave. And the receiving store, only when they arrive. If Kallakurichi adds the oil before it arrives, it can promise customers oil that's still on the road. And if both stores count it, the same twelve bottles exist twice.
owner-6-read: Read each row. Ulundurpet had twenty-four, sent twelve, and has twelve left. Kallakurichi had seven, and receives twelve, making nineteen. And the Villupuram warehouse doesn't change at all. Tap the button when you've read it.
owner-6-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Stock.
owner-6-when: When does Kallakurichi's stock go up by twelve?
owner-7-actor: Every row shows the actor as Current operator. So what do you tell the accountant?
owner-7-cols: Which columns does the export contain?
owner-7-done: Good. You gave real evidence, and you were honest about what it doesn't show. That's what makes evidence trustworthy.
owner-7-export: Choose Export C S V. The file downloads to your computer.
owner-7-intro: Your accountant calls. She'd like evidence of today's decisions and cash events. You could send screenshots, or type out a summary. But neither can be checked against the system. An export is different. It's a copy of the record, at one moment in time. Someone outside the system can check every decision, without being given the power to change anything.
owner-7-ready: Make sure you're viewing as Business owner, and open Audit.
